title: On one hand, on the other: contrast connectors

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *sin embargo*, *no obstante* and *aunque* from B1 Unit 1. They link two ideas that pull in different directions. The market reforms are full of such pairs: a gain on one side, a cost on the other.

items.spanish: El modelo ayudó a crear fábricas; sin embargo, muchos lo consideraron agotado.
items.english: The model helped create factories; however, many considered it exhausted.

items.spanish: La inflación bajó mucho; no obstante, el peso fijo hizo más difícil exportar.
items.english: Inflation fell a lot; nevertheless, the fixed peso made exporting harder.

items.spanish: Los gobiernos dieron la bienvenida a la inversión extranjera, aunque antes muchos la miraban con desconfianza.
items.english: Governments welcomed foreign investment, although before many looked at it with distrust.

items.spanish: Los consumidores compraban más barato; sin embargo, muchas fábricas pequeñas cerraron.
items.english: Consumers bought more cheaply; however, many small factories closed.

sections.content: *Sin embargo* and *no obstante* usually start a new clause and take a comma after them; *no obstante* is more formal. *Aunque* joins two clauses in one sentence. Do not use *por eso* for a contrast: *por eso* gives a result.
